topics.title: Greetings
topics.description: Say hello, goodbye, and how are you

guide.intro: Mandarin has only a handful of greetings to learn — but the tones really matter. Here's what to know before you start.

sections.text: The four tones

Every Mandarin syllable has one of four pitched tones (plus a neutral "fifth" tone). The same syllable means different things depending on tone — so "mā", "má", "mǎ", and "mà" are four different words.
Hello: 你好 (nǐ hǎo)
你 means "you" and 好 means "good". Put them together for "you good?" — the standard hello, usable any time of day.
When two 3rd-tone syllables stack like nǐ hǎo, the first one shifts up to a 2nd tone in speech (ní hǎo). It still gets written as nǐ hǎo.
你 (nǐ) vs 您 (nín)
您 is the polite form of "you" — used with elders, customers, and strangers. 你 is everyday/casual. Both pronounced almost the same.

rows.translation: Hi there.
Hello (formal).
Hello, teacher.

sections.text: How are you?
To turn a statement into a yes/no question, just add 吗 (ma) at the end. So 你好 ("you're good") + 吗 = 你好吗? ("are you good?").

rows.translation: How are you?
I am very good.
Not bad.

topics.title: Numbers
topics.description: Count, ask how many, give your age

guide.intro: Mandarin numbers are wonderfully regular — once you know 1 to 10 and the word for "ten", you can build every number up to 99.

sections.text: One to ten
Building 11–99
After ten, numbers are built like math problems. Read characters left to right, multiplying anything before 十 and adding anything after.
Same trick goes further: 一百 (one hundred), 一千 (one thousand), 一万 (ten thousand) — but Chinese groups large numbers in 万 (10,000) rather than thousands.
Two: 二 vs 两
Mandarin has two words for "two". 二 (èr) is the digit — used in counting, math, and phone numbers. 两 (liǎng) means "a pair of" — used before measure words and quantities.

rows.translation: twenty (the number)
two people (with measure word)

sections.text: Asking how many
几 (jǐ) asks "how many?" for small expected counts (under ~10). 多少 (duō shǎo) asks "how much/many?" for any quantity, including money and big numbers.

rows.translation: How old are you? (to a child)
How much money?

topics.title: Basics
topics.description: Yes, no, I, you, this, that

guide.intro: Mandarin has no verb conjugation, no plural endings, no genders, and no articles. Once you know the word order, the language gets out of your way.

sections.text: Word order: subject – verb – object
Just like English, a basic sentence puts the subject first, the verb second, and the object last.

rows.translation: I drink tea.
He eats rice.
I love you.

sections.text: Pronouns are simple
他 (he) and 她 (she) are pronounced exactly the same — only the writing changes. In speech, listeners use context.
The verb 是 (shì)
是 means "to be" — but only for nouns connecting to other nouns ("I am a student"). For adjectives, you don't use 是; you use 很 (hěn) instead, which means "very" but is often a placeholder.

rows.translation: I am a student.
I am good. (no 是!)

sections.text: Negation: 不 vs 没
Use 不 (bù) for negating present and future actions, and for adjectives. Use 没 (méi) for past actions and for the verb 有 ("to have").

rows.source: 我 不 喝 茶。
rows.translation: I don't drink tea.

rows.source: 我 没 有 钱。
rows.translation: I don't have money.

sections.text: No tenses!
Mandarin verbs do not change form for past, present, or future. Time is shown by adding a time word (yesterday, tomorrow) or particles like 了 (le) for completion.

rows.source: 昨天 我 吃 米饭。
rows.translation: Yesterday I ate rice.

rows.source: 明天 我 吃 米饭。
rows.translation: Tomorrow I will eat rice.

topics.title: Common verbs
topics.description: Go, eat, want, like, see, listen

guide.intro: Mandarin verbs never change form. The same character is used for all persons and all times — context (and time words) does the heavy lifting.

sections.text: One verb, every form
Compare with English: "go / goes / went / will go" — Mandarin uses 去 for all of them. The action stays put; you add words around it.

rows.translation: I go / I am going.
He goes.
We go.
I went yesterday.

sections.text: Want vs. would-like: 要 / 想 / 喜欢
These three look interchangeable in English but have a clear pecking order in Mandarin.

rows: I want / I will (decisive, ordering food)
I would like / I am thinking about

rows.translation: I want coffee. (I'll have)

rows.source: 我 想 喝 咖啡。
rows.translation: I would like to drink coffee.
I like coffee.

sections.text: Completion: the 了 particle
Adding 了 (le) after a verb signals an action is finished. It's the closest thing Mandarin has to past tense — but it's really an aspect marker, not a tense.

rows.translation: I am eating.

rows.source: 我 吃 了 饭。
rows.translation: I ate. / I have eaten.

sections.text: Don't sprinkle 了 everywhere — for adjectives ("I am happy") or stative verbs, you don't use it. Save it for completed actions.

topics.title: Time
topics.description: Days, hours, and when things happen

guide.intro: Time words go at the start of a sentence or right after the subject — never at the end like English. "Tomorrow I go" is the natural Mandarin order.

sections.text: Days are math
Days of the week are 星期 (xīngqī, "week") + the digit. So 星期一 is week-1 (Monday), 星期二 is week-2 (Tuesday), and so on through 星期六. Sunday is the odd one out: 星期天 or 星期日.
Telling time
Hours use 点 (diǎn, "o'clock"), minutes use 分 (fēn). Half-past is 半 (bàn). "Quarter" is 一刻 (yí kè) for :15 and 三刻 for :45.

rows.translation: 3 o'clock

sections.text: Time-words come first
In Mandarin, time goes before the verb. Compare:

rows.source: 我 明天 去 学校。
rows.translation: I am going to school tomorrow.

rows.source: 他 今天 不 来。
rows.translation: He is not coming today.

sections.text: A handy memory trick: Chinese says time in big-to-small order — year, month, day, hour, minute. The opposite of how dates are spoken in English.

topics.title: Questions
topics.description: Who, what, when, why, how

guide.intro: Mandarin questions are unusually friendly to learners — there's no auxiliary "do/does", no inversion. The word order stays the same as a statement.

sections.text: The 吗 particle
For yes/no questions, take a statement and add 吗 (ma) at the end. That's it. No reordering, no auxiliary verb.

rows.translation: You drink tea.

rows.source: 你 喝 茶 吗？
rows.translation: Do you drink tea?

sections.text: Question words stay put
For information questions (who, what, where), put the question word exactly where the answer would go. No fronting like English.

rows.translation: Who are you? (You are who?)
What are you drinking?
Where are you?
Why is he coming?

sections.text: Common question words
A-not-A questions
A second way to ask yes/no questions: repeat the verb with 不 between. It's a touch more direct than 吗.

rows.source: 你 是不是 学生？
rows.translation: Are you a student or not?
Do you drink tea or not?

sections.text: Don't mix patterns: 你是不是学生吗？ is wrong. Pick one of the two question forms.

topics.title: Completed actions
topics.description: 了 for what just happened, 过 for what you've ever done

guide.intro: A1 introduced 了 briefly. A2 is where it really earns its keep. There are also two siblings to learn — 过 (experience) and 还没 (not yet) — that round out talking about the past.

sections.text: 了 — completed action
Tack 了 onto a verb to mark that the action is finished. It's the closest thing Mandarin has to a past tense, but technically it's an aspect marker — the action is complete, not necessarily long ago.

rows.translation: I am eating.

rows.source: 我 吃 了 饭。
rows.translation: I ate / I have eaten.
He came / he's here.

sections.text: Negation: 还没 (not yet)
Don't pair 了 with 不/没. To say "haven't done it", drop 了 and use 还没 (hái méi):

rows.translation: I haven't eaten yet.
He hasn't come yet.

sections.text: 过 — experience marker
过 (guò) tags a verb as "have you ever done this in your life?" — it's about experience, not completion. Compare:

rows.source: 我 吃 过 北京 烤鸭。
rows.translation: I have eaten Peking duck (sometime).

rows.source: 我 吃 了 北京 烤鸭。
rows.translation: I ate Peking duck (just now).

sections.text: Rule of thumb: 了 = the action is wrapped up. 过 = at some point in your life this happened. They occasionally co-occur but you'll mostly pick one.

sections.text: Money words
Spoken Chinese uses 块 (kuài) for the main currency unit; written and formal Chinese uses 元 (yuán). They're the same value — like "buck" vs "dollar". 毛 (máo) and 分 (fēn) are tenths and hundredths.

topics.title: Comparisons
topics.description: A is bigger than B — the 比 pattern

guide.intro: English uses "-er" or "more" for comparisons. Mandarin uses 比 (bǐ) — a single particle that does the same job, with a fixed word order: A 比 B + adjective.

sections.text: Basic pattern: A 比 B + adjective

rows.source: 我 比 他 高。
rows.translation: I am taller than him.

rows.source: 苹果 比 香蕉 便宜。
rows.translation: Apples are cheaper than bananas.

rows.source: 今天 比 昨天 热。
rows.translation: Today is hotter than yesterday.

sections.text: Don't add 很 / 不 / 是 to a 比 sentence. "我 比 他 很 高" is wrong — drop 很. The comparison itself does the work.
Even more: 更
Add 更 (gèng, "even more") before the adjective when comparing to an already-strong baseline:

rows.source: 他 比 我 更 高。
rows.translation: He is even taller than me.

sections.text: The most: 最
最 (zuì) before an adjective means "the most". No 比 needed — it's a superlative.

rows.translation: He is the tallest.

rows.source: 我 最 喜欢 茶。
rows.translation: I like tea the most.

sections.text: Negative: A 没有 B + adjective
To say "A is NOT as ___ as B", flip to 没有 (méi yǒu, "doesn't have"):

rows.source: 我 没有 他 高。
rows.translation: I am not as tall as him.

guide.intro: Up to now most sentences have been one thought. A2 is where you start chaining: "I went and then I ate", "It rained but I went", "I'm tired because I worked". Mandarin makes this easy — a small set of connectors does most of the heavy lifting.

topics.title: The 把 construction
topics.description: Putting the object first to talk about what you do TO it

guide.intro: 把 (bǎ) is one of the most distinctive features of Mandarin grammar. It moves the object before the verb to say "take X and do something to it". You'll hear it constantly — and English doesn't have a clean equivalent.

sections.text: The basic shape

Normal Chinese order is Subject–Verb–Object. With 把, you reorder to Subject–把–Object–Verb–(extra). The "extra" part is crucial — 把 sentences almost never end on a bare verb. There has to be a result, location, or change attached.

rows: 我 把 门 关 上
他 把 苹果 吃 了
请 放 书 在 桌子 上
请 把 书 放 在 桌子 上

sections.text: When to use 把
Use 把 when you want to emphasize what HAPPENS TO a specific, known object — moving it, finishing it, changing it, putting it somewhere. Both speaker and listener know which object you mean.

rows.source: 我 把 作业 做 完 了。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ bǎ zuòyè zuò wán le.
rows.translation: I finished the homework.

rows.source: 请 把 窗户 打 开。
rows.translation: Please open the window.

rows.source: 他 把 杯子 打 破 了。
rows.pinyin: Tā bǎ bēizi dǎ pò le.
rows.translation: He broke the cup.

sections.text: If you can't say what HAPPENS TO the object, don't use 把. "我 把 苹果 喜欢" is wrong — 喜欢 (like) doesn't change the apple.
What can't follow 把
把 needs a verb that physically affects the object. Verbs that don't qualify: feeling/perception verbs (爱, 喜欢, 觉得, 知道), existence verbs (有, 是), and most stative or motion-only verbs (来, 去, 走).

rows.source: 我 喜欢 这 本 书。
rows.translation: I like this book. (NOT 我 把 这 本 书 喜欢)
He knows the answer. (NOT 他 把 答案 知道)

sections.text: Negation: 没 / 不 goes BEFORE 把

rows.source: 我 没 把 作业 做 完。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ méi bǎ zuòyè zuò wán.
rows.translation: I didn't finish the homework.

rows.source: 请 不要 把 门 关 上。
rows.pinyin: Qǐng bú yào bǎ mén guān shàng.

topics.title: The 被 passive
topics.description: When something happens TO the subject — usually unpleasantly

guide.intro: 被 (bèi) is the passive marker — "got / was done by". It's the mirror image of 把: where 把 puts the actor first and the patient mid-sentence, 被 puts the patient (victim) first.

sections.text: The basic shape
Pattern: Patient + 被 + (Agent) + Verb + result. The agent is optional — drop it if it's unknown or obvious.

rows.source: 我 的 手机 被 偷 了。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī bèi tōu le.
rows.translation: My phone was stolen. (no agent)

rows.source: 杯子 被 他 打 破 了。
rows.pinyin: Bēizi bèi tā dǎ pò le.
rows.translation: The cup was broken by him.

rows.source: 钱 被 老板 拿走 了。
rows.pinyin: Qián bèi lǎobǎn ná zǒu le.
rows.translation: The money was taken by the boss.

sections.text: 把 vs 被 — same event, different POV

rows: 他 把 杯子 打 破 了
杯子 被 他 打 破 了
小偷 偷 了 我 的 手机
我 的 手机 被 (小偷) 偷 了

sections.text: Mandarin's 被 has a slightly negative or unfortunate flavor — it's used much more often for bad things (got stolen, broken, scolded) than for neutral or good ones. Sentences like "I was praised" (我 被 表扬 了) work but feel marked.
叫 / 让 — informal alternatives
In speech, 叫 (jiào) or 让 (ràng) often replace 被. They sound more casual — but unlike 被, they REQUIRE an agent.

rows.source: 我 的 钱 让 他 拿走 了。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ de qián ràng tā ná zǒu le.
rows.translation: My money got taken by him.

rows.source: 他 叫 老师 批评 了。
rows.translation: He got scolded by the teacher.

sections.text: Negation
Same as 把 — put 没 BEFORE 被.

rows.source: 我 的 手机 没 被 偷。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī méi bèi tōu.
rows.translation: My phone wasn't stolen.

sections.text: Two flavors of 了
Mandarin uses 了 in two distinct slots, and 把 / 被 sentences often need both. Knowing which is which is the difference between a complete sentence and a fragment.

rows: Something is now different / new situation

rows.source: 他 吃 了 三 个 苹果。
rows.pinyin: Tā chī le sān ge píngguǒ.
rows.translation: He ate three apples. (perfective 了₁ — action complete)
It's raining now. (sentence 了₂ — change of state, didn't use to be)

rows.source: 已经 下 了 三 天 雨 了。
rows.pinyin: Yǐjīng xià le sān tiān yǔ le.
rows.translation: It's been raining for three days. (BOTH 了 — completed duration AND ongoing relevance)

sections.text: Quick test: if the 了 hugs the verb (verb 了 object), it's 了₁. If the 了 is at the very end of the sentence, it's 了₂. Same character, different jobs.

topics.title: Giving with 给
topics.description: 给 as both "give" and a coverb meaning "for / to"

guide.intro: 给 (gěi) wears two hats. As a main verb it means "give". As a coverb sitting before another verb, it marks the recipient or beneficiary — "for someone", "to someone". Both uses are everywhere.

sections.text: 给 as main verb — "give"
Pattern: Subject + 给 + recipient + thing. Two objects in a row, recipient first.

rows.source: 我 给 他 一 本 书。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ gěi tā yì běn shū.
rows.translation: I gave him a book.

rows.source: 妈妈 给 我 钱。
rows.translation: Mom gave me money.

sections.text: 给 as coverb — "for / to"
Sandwiched before another verb, 给 marks who benefits or receives the action. Pattern: Subject + 给 + recipient + verb + object.

rows.source: 我 给 你 买 了 一 杯 咖啡。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ gěi nǐ mǎi le yì bēi kāfēi.
rows.translation: I bought you a coffee. (the buying is FOR you)

rows.source: 他 给 妈妈 打 电话。
rows.translation: He's calling mom. (the call is TO mom)

rows.source: 请 给 我 介绍 一下。
rows.translation: Please introduce (it) to me.

sections.text: Notice how 给 you 买 (buy for you) and 给 妈妈 打 电话 (call mom) both keep 给 + person BEFORE the main verb. English flips this around — Chinese is rigid about the order.

topics.title: How well? — 得 complement
topics.description: Modify a verb with how it was done — 得 + adjective

guide.intro: 得 (de) lets you describe the manner or degree of an action: not WHAT you did, but HOW WELL or HOW MUCH. It's the closest Mandarin gets to English adverbs.

sections.text: The basic pattern
Pattern: Subject + Verb + 得 + (very) + Adjective. Note the position of 很 — almost always required to keep the sentence sounding natural.

rows.source: 他 跑 得 很 快。
rows.translation: He runs very fast.

rows.source: 她 唱 得 很 好。
rows.translation: She sings very well.

rows.source: 我 睡 得 不 好。
rows.translation: I didn't sleep well.

sections.text: When the verb has an object
If your verb takes an object, you have to repeat the verb. Mandarin can't have an object AND a 得 phrase on the same verb. Pattern: Subject + Verb + Object, Verb + 得 + adjective.

rows.source: 他 说 中文 说 得 很 好。
rows.pinyin: Tā shuō Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo.

rows.pinyin: Tā xiě zì xiě de hěn piàoliang.

sections.text: Common mistake: "他 说 中文 得 很 好" — wrong. The verb has to repeat. Or you can drop the object: "他 中文 说 得 很 好" also works.
Three different 得 / 的 / 地

rows: after a verb: how it was done
走 得 慢 — walks slowly

sections.text: All three are pronounced "de" (neutral tone) — only writing distinguishes them. Pay attention to position: 的 between nouns, 地 before verbs, 得 after verbs.
Negation: not 不 before 得 — 不 before the adjective

rows.source: 他 跑 得 不 快。
rows.translation: He doesn't run fast.

rows.source: 我 唱 得 不 好。
rows.translation: I don't sing well.

topics.title: Opinions & agreement
topics.description: I think, I believe, I agree — saying what you reckon

guide.intro: B1 means saying more than "I like" or "I want". You need ways to express opinions softly, agree, disagree, and ask people what THEY think. Three verbs do the heavy lifting: 觉得, 认为, and 看.

sections.text: 觉得 — feel / think (everyday)
觉得 (jué de) is the workhorse — "I feel / think that...". Use it for any soft, personal opinion. By far the most common in conversation.

rows.source: 我 觉得 这 个 电影 很 好。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ juéde zhè ge diànyǐng hěn hǎo.
rows.translation: I think this movie is good.

rows.source: 你 觉得 怎么样？
rows.translation: What do you think?

sections.text: 认为 — believe / hold (more formal)
认为 (rèn wéi) is firmer and more written — "I hold the view that...". Right for opinions on bigger issues, news, business, debate.

rows.source: 我 认为 这 个 计划 不 行。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ rènwéi zhè ge jìhuà bù xíng.
rows.translation: I don't think this plan will work.

rows.source: 专家 认为 经济 会 好转。
rows.translation: Experts believe the economy will improve.

sections.text: 看 — see / view (informal opinion ask)
看 (kàn) literally means "look", but "你 看 …" idiomatically means "in your view, …". Used to gently ask someone's take.

rows.source: 你 看 我 该 怎么 办？
rows.pinyin: Nǐ kàn wǒ gāi zěnme bàn?
rows.translation: What do you think I should do?

rows.source: 我 看 应该 没 问题。
rows.translation: I think it should be fine.

sections.text: Agreeing & disagreeing
Chinese conversation tends to soften disagreement. "我 不 太 同意" (I don't really agree) is gentler and more common than a flat "不 同意".

topics.title: Telling a story
topics.description: Sequencing past events with 着 and directional verbs

guide.intro: When you narrate a story you need ways to set the scene ("she was sitting"), describe motion ("he walked in"), and string events together. 着 handles ongoing states; directional complements like 上来 and 下去 handle motion in space.

sections.text: 着 — ongoing state
着 (zhe) attached to a verb means "in the state of doing". It's NOT the same as English -ing — 着 emphasizes a held position or background condition, often setting the scene.

rows.translation: He is standing. (in a standing state)
The door is open. (held open)

rows.source: 她 笑 着 说。
rows.translation: She said with a smile. (smiling-while-speaking)

sections.text: 着 vs 在: 在 means "actively doing right now" ("我 在 吃饭" — I'm eating). 着 means "in this state" ("门 开 着" — the door's open). For narration, 着 sets the scene; 在 reports a live action.
Directional complements: 上 / 下 / 进 / 出 / 来 / 去
Six little words combine into rich verbs of motion. Pair a base direction (up/down/in/out) with 来 (toward speaker) or 去 (away from speaker).

rows.source: 他 走 进来 了。
rows.translation: He walked in.

rows.source: 她 跑 出去 了。
rows.translation: She ran out.
Please come up.

sections.text: Figurative directionals — 起来 / 下去 / 出来
Directional complements stretch beyond physical motion. Attached to non-motion verbs, they signal phase or aspect: starting, continuing, or coming-to-clarity.

rows: 看 起来 很 累 — looks tired

rows.source: 我 终于 想 出来 了。
rows.translation: I finally figured it out.

rows.source: 请 你 说 下 去。
rows.translation: Please keep talking.

rows.source: 他 突然 笑 起来 了。
rows.translation: He suddenly started to laugh.

sections.text: Sequencing words
A2's 然后 still works, but B1 stories add 先...再... (first...then...), 最后 (finally), 突然 (suddenly), and 后来 (afterward — for events further apart).

rows.source: 我 先 吃饭，再 看 电影。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ xiān chīfàn, zài kàn diànyǐng.
rows.translation: First I'll eat, then watch a movie.
It suddenly started to rain.

rows.source: 后来 他 搬 走 了。
rows.translation: Afterward, he moved away.

guide.intro: At B2 you stop just stating opinions and start structuring them — adding nuance, layering reasons, and naming the side you fall on. Three patterns will carry most of your opinion-talk for the rest of your Chinese life: 不仅…而且 (not only…but also), 我觉得…比较 (I think…relatively), and 一方面…另一方面 (on one hand…on the other).

sections.text: 不仅…而且 — not only…but also

不仅 (bù jǐn) sets up the first half of a two-part claim, and 而且 (ér qiě) adds the second, usually stronger, point. The two halves can share a subject (which sits in front) or have different subjects (which sit after each particle).

rows.source: 他不仅会说中文，而且会说日语。
rows.pinyin: Tā bù jǐn huì shuō Zhōngwén, ér qiě huì shuō Rìyǔ.
rows.translation: He not only speaks Chinese, but also Japanese.

rows.source: 这家餐厅不仅便宜，而且很好吃。
rows.pinyin: Zhè jiā cāntīng bù jǐn piányi, ér qiě hěn hǎo chī.
rows.translation: This restaurant is not only cheap but also delicious.

rows.source: 不仅我喜欢他，而且我妹妹也喜欢他。
rows.pinyin: Bù jǐn wǒ xǐhuan tā, ér qiě wǒ mèimei yě xǐhuan tā.
rows.translation: Not only do I like him, but my sister does too.

sections.text: Common mistake: dropping 而且 and joining with a comma. In Mandarin, 不仅 always pairs with 而且 (or 也 / 还). "他不仅高，帅" sounds incomplete.
Softening: 我觉得 + 比较

比较 (bǐ jiào) means "relatively" or "fairly" — it takes the edge off an opinion the way "kind of" does in English. Pair it with 我觉得 (wǒ jué de, "I feel") for a polite, hedged tone that won't sound confrontational.

rows.source: 我觉得这个想法比较有意思。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ jué de zhè ge xiǎngfǎ bǐ jiào yǒu yì si.
rows.translation: I think this idea is fairly interesting.

rows.source: 我觉得他说的比较有道理。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ jué de tā shuō de bǐ jiào yǒu dào lǐ.
rows.translation: I think what he said makes a fair amount of sense.

sections.text: Two sides: 一方面…另一方面
Use 一方面 (yī fāng miàn)…另一方面 (lìng yī fāng miàn) to lay out two sides of the same issue — the closest Mandarin gets to "on one hand…on the other hand".

rows.source: 一方面工作很累，另一方面工资也不高。
rows.pinyin: Yī fāng miàn gōng zuò hěn lèi, lìng yī fāng miàn gōng zī yě bù gāo.
rows.translation: On one hand the work is tiring, on the other hand the pay isn't great either.

guide.intro: 越…越 (yuè…yuè) is one of the most useful patterns at B2 — and one of the prettiest. It means "the more X, the more Y". You'll hear it everywhere from weather reports to op-eds. This topic uses environmental issues as the playground for it.

sections.text: 越…越 — the more…the more
The pattern is fixed: 越 + verb/adjective, 越 + verb/adjective. The two halves can share a subject (which sits at the front) or have different subjects.

rows.pinyin: Tiān qì yuè lái yuè rè.
rows.translation: The weather is getting hotter and hotter.

rows.pinyin: Tā yuè shuō yuè shēng qì.
rows.translation: The more he talked, the angrier he got.
The rain came down heavier and heavier.

sections.text: 越来越 — getting X-er
越来越 (yuè lái yuè) is the most common form: "more and more". It always sits in front of an adjective or stative verb, and signals a trend over time.

rows.pinyin: Kōng qì yuè lái yuè chà.
rows.translation: The air is getting worse and worse.

rows.pinyin: Huán bǎo yuè lái yuè zhòng yào.
rows.translation: Environmental protection is getting more and more important.

sections.text: Don't add 很 between 越来越 and the adjective. "越来越很热" is wrong — 越来越 already does the intensifying.
Two-subject form
When the two halves have different subjects, both subjects appear inside the pattern, after each 越:

rows.source: 天气越冷，我越想吃火锅。
rows.pinyin: Tiān qì yuè lěng, wǒ yuè xiǎng chī huǒ guō.
rows.translation: The colder the weather, the more I want hotpot.

guide.intro: B2 emotions need B2 grammar. The patterns 即使…也 (even if…still) and 尽管 (although) let you say things like "even if I'm tired, I'll still finish" and "although I'm sad, I'm okay" — exactly the kind of nuance you start needing once you go past 我很高兴.

sections.text: 即使…也 — even if…still

即使 (jí shǐ) introduces a hypothetical or extreme condition; the second half always uses 也 (yě, "still") or 还 (hái) to mark that the result holds regardless. Without that 也, the sentence sounds incomplete to a native ear.

sections.text: 即使 is for hypotheticals ("even if it rains") — events that may or may not happen. 即便 (jí biàn) is a slightly more formal synonym you'll see in writing.
尽管…但是 — although

尽管 (jǐn guǎn) introduces an actual fact (not a hypothetical), and 但是 (dàn shì, "but") or 还是 (hái shi, "still") marks the contrasting follow-up. Use 尽管 when the first clause is true and the second clause is the surprise.

rows.translation: Although it was raining, he still went running.

您 (nín) is the polite "you". You'll use it for clients, customers, elders, professors, and strangers in any service context. In groups, 您们 is rare — most speakers stay with 您 (singular) or use 各位 (everyone).

topics.title: Business Chinese
topics.description: Meetings, negotiation, and formal correspondence

guide.intro: Business Mandarin lives in a register far above everyday speech. The same idea you'd say with 因为...所以 over coffee gets dressed up with 鉴于... 因此 in a meeting. Three habits define the register: connectives that tie clauses together, nominalized topics with 至于, and a default to 您 / 贵 honorifics.

sections.text: Formal causal connectives

Casual Chinese uses 因为 X 所以 Y. In formal writing and meetings, you upgrade to 鉴于 X，因此 Y ("in view of X, therefore Y") or 由于 X，故 Y ("owing to X, hence Y"). 因此 and 故 are interchangeable for "therefore", but 故 sounds bookish.

rows.source: 鉴于市场环境的变化，我们因此调整了战略。
rows.pinyin: Jiànyú shìchǎng huánjìng de biànhuà, wǒmen yīncǐ tiáozhěng le zhànlüè.
rows.translation: In view of market changes, we have therefore adjusted our strategy.

rows.source: 由于成本上升，公司因此决定提价。
rows.pinyin: Yóuyú chéngběn shàngshēng, gōngsī yīncǐ juédìng tíjià.
rows.translation: Owing to rising costs, the company has accordingly decided to raise prices.

rows.source: 因为成本上升，所以我们涨价了。
rows.pinyin: Yīnwèi chéngběn shàngshēng, suǒyǐ wǒmen zhǎngjià le.
rows.translation: Because costs rose, we raised prices. (casual)

sections.text: 然而 vs 但是 — "however"
但是 works in any register. 然而 is the formal cousin you reach for in reports, op-eds, and presentations. 不过 sits in between — written Chinese friendly but not stiff.

rows: Strong contrast in essays, news, reports.

sections.text: 至于 — topic shift

至于 X ("as for X") moves the spotlight to a new sub-topic and is heavily used in structured talks. The phrase always introduces a fresh clause and is followed by a comma. Think of it as the spoken equivalent of a slide transition.

rows.source: 营收方面我们超出预期。至于成本，仍需进一步控制。
rows.pinyin: Yíngshōu fāngmiàn wǒmen chāochū yùqī. Zhìyú chéngběn, réng xū jìnyībù kòngzhì.
rows.translation: On revenue we exceeded expectations. As for costs, they still need to be controlled further.

rows.source: 至于您提到的合作方式，我们下周再深入讨论。
rows.pinyin: Zhìyú nín tídào de hézuò fāngshì, wǒmen xiàzhōu zài shēnrù tǎolùn.
rows.translation: As for the form of cooperation you mentioned, let us discuss it in depth next week.

sections.text: 贵 — honorific prefix

贵 ("honored") attaches to nouns referring to the other party's affiliations: 贵公司 (your company), 贵校 (your school), 贵姓 (your honored surname). Use 贵 anywhere a respectful tone is owed; in return, refer to your own side with the humble 敝 (敝公司 "my humble company") or simply 我方 ("our side").
Mixing registers will make you sound off. Once you open a meeting with 贵公司, stay in formal mode: keep using 您, swap 但是 for 然而, and lean on 至于 for transitions.

guide.intro: Academic Chinese is dense, nominalized, and emphasis-heavy. Two structures dominate: 是...的 to spotlight one component of an established fact, and nominalization with 的 / 来说 / 而言 to package whole clauses as topics. Master these and your writing instantly sounds academic.

sections.text: 是...的 — emphasis on a known event

When the listener already knows the action happened and you want to highlight when, where, how, or who did it, wrap that element in 是...的. The 是 sits before the highlighted phrase; 的 closes the sentence.

rows.translation: He came. (neutral statement)
It was yesterday that he came. (when)

rows.pinyin: Tā shì cóng Běijīng lái de.
rows.translation: It is from Beijing that he came. (where)

rows.pinyin: Zhè běn shū shì èr líng yī bā nián chūbǎn de.
rows.translation: This book was published in 2018. (focus on the year)

sections.text: 是...的 only works for events the listener already accepts as fact. If you're announcing fresh news, use 了 instead — 是...的 would sound oddly defensive.
Nominalization with 的话 / 来说 / 而言

Academic writing turns clauses into topic NPs. 对 X 来说 / 对 X 而言 means "as far as X is concerned". 就 X 而言 raises the formality further. These structures let you front a scoped premise before delivering an argument.

rows.source: 对发展中国家来说，气候变化是巨大的挑战。
rows.pinyin: Duì fāzhǎn zhōng guójiā lái shuō, qìhòu biànhuà shì jùdà de tiǎozhàn.
rows.translation: For developing countries, climate change is a huge challenge.

rows.source: 就经济效益而言，这个方案最为合理。
rows.pinyin: Jiù jīngjì xiàoyì ér yán, zhège fāng'àn zuì wéi hélǐ.
rows.translation: In terms of economic benefit, this plan is the most reasonable.

rows.source: 如果按这个标准的话，我们都不合格。
rows.pinyin: Rúguǒ àn zhège biāozhǔn de huà, wǒmen dōu bù hégé.
rows.translation: If we go by this standard, none of us qualify.

sections.text: Hedging your claims
Academic Chinese hedges constantly. 似乎 (it seems), 可能 (possibly), 在一定程度上 (to a certain extent), and 总的来说 (generally speaking) are the four pillars. Stack them to soften strong claims.

exercises.prompt: What does "她是去年从英国回来的" emphasize?
options: When and where she returned from
exercises.answer: When and where she returned from
exercises.explanation: 是...的 highlights the time (去年) and origin (从英国); the listener already knows she returned.

exercises.prompt: Build "This theory was first proposed by Einstein"
exercises.answer: 这个 理论 是 爱因斯坦 最早 提出 的

exercises.prompt: Pick the correct emphasis sentence for "It was in 1949 that the People's Republic was founded."

中华人民共和国1949年成立了
中华人民共和国成立1949年
中华人民共和国是1949年成立
exercises.answer: 中华人民共和国是1949年成立的
exercises.explanation: 是...的 frames 1949 as the focused year; the other options either drop 是, drop 的, or scramble the word order.

exercises.prompt: Pick the correct word: "这篇论文 ___ 王教授写的" (focus: who wrote it)
exercises.explanation: 是...的 fronts "by Professor Wang" as the focus. 被 would create a passive but mismatch with 的; 把 needs a disposed object after it; 在 marks location, not agent focus.

exercises.prompt: Which is most formal?
exercises.explanation: 对...而言 is the formal academic version of 对...来说; both go further than 我觉得.

exercises.answer: It is well known to all

exercises.answer: From this we can see / it follows that

topics.title: Art & literature
topics.description: Read poems, discuss films, appreciate calligraphy

guide.intro: Classical Chinese threads through modern writing in three little words: 之, 其, 所. They look intimidating but they're not new grammar — they're compressed forms of structures you already know. Recognize them and most literary and academic Chinese opens up.

sections.text: 之 — the literary 的
之 (zhī) is what 的 used to be. In modern Chinese it survives in fixed expressions and titles. Wherever you see 之, mentally substitute 的. The structure 名词 + 之 + 名词 = "X's Y" or "Y of X".

rows.translation: The beauty of China (= 中国的美)
The path to success
All in all ("to sum up and speak of it")

rows.pinyin: Yì jǔ liǎng dé zhī shì
rows.translation: Something that kills two birds with one stone

sections.text: 其 — "its / their / his / her"
其 (qí) is the literary third-person possessive — equivalent to 它的 / 他的 / 她的 / 他们的, depending on context. You'll meet it in essays, instructions, and idioms.

rows.translation: Its (the) result is shocking.
The company and its employees
Especially ("particularly its [case]")
Each takes what they need

sections.text: 所 — turning verbs into nouns

所 (suǒ) sits before a verb to nominalize the object: 所 + 动词 = "that which is V-ed". The full pattern is often 名词 + 所 + 动词 + 的 + 名词 = "the X that N V's". It feels ancient but appears constantly in titles and formal speech.

rows.translation: What I have seen (literally: that which I saw)
The efforts we have made
As is universally known
As reason dictates / naturally

sections.text: You almost never need to write 之/其/所 yourself in everyday Chinese. The goal is recognition: when you see 其, your brain swaps in 它的; when you see 所...的, you read it as "the thing that is V-ed".

exercises.prompt: Match the genre
What does "这本小说情节曲折" mean?
options: This novel has a winding / twisty plot
exercises.answer: This novel has a winding / twisty plot
exercises.explanation: 曲折 = winding, turning — a positive description of an engaging plot.

exercises.prompt: Build "The hero's character is portrayed very vividly"
exercises.answer: 主人公 的 性格 刻画 得 非常 生动

exercises.prompt: "这部作品堪称经典" — 堪称 means "___ to be called"
exercises.explanation: 堪称经典 ("worthy of being called a classic") is a stock praise phrase.

exercises.prompt: Match the film term
What does "票房口碑双丰收" mean?
options: Box office and word-of-mouth both succeed
exercises.answer: Box office and word-of-mouth both succeed
exercises.explanation: 口碑 = word-of-mouth/reputation; 双丰收 = double harvest — high praise for a movie.

exercises.prompt: Build "This film reflects deep social issues"
exercises.answer: 这 部 电影 反映 了 深刻 的 社会 问题

exercises.prompt: "这部电影感人至深" — 感人至深 means deeply ___
exercises.explanation: 感人至深 = literally "moves people to the depths".

lessons.title: Classical traces — 之 / 其
lessons.description: Recognize literary leftovers in modern writing

exercises.prompt: In "中国之美", 之 functions as ___
exercises.explanation: 之 in 中国之美 is the modifier-marker (= 的), linking 中国 to 美 — "the beauty of China".

exercises.prompt: Match the 之 / 其 expression
Rewrite "该书及它的译本" in literary register: "该书及 ___ 译本"
exercises.explanation: 其 = 它的 — the literary possessive used in formal writing.

exercises.prompt: What does "成功之道" mean?
exercises.explanation: 之 = 的; 道 = way / path.

exercises.prompt: What does "我所喜欢的书" mean?
exercises.explanation: 所 + verb + 的 + noun = the [noun] that [subject] [verbs].

exercises.prompt: Match the 所 idiom to its meaning

pairs.right: Naturally / as a matter of course

exercises.prompt: Build "What he said is exactly what I think"
exercises.answer: 他 所 说 的 正是 我 所 想 的

exercises.prompt: "理所当然" means "as ___ would have it / naturally"
exercises.explanation: 理 (reason) + 所 + 当然 — "that which reason makes natural".

topics.title: News & journalism
topics.description: Read headlines, parse op-eds, follow current events

guide.intro: News Chinese is its own dialect — short, dense, and heavy with cause-effect connectives. Two patterns dominate explanatory writing: 之所以 X 是因为 Y for reverse-order causation, and 不仅 X 而且 Y for stacking points. Get fluent in these and headlines stop being puzzles.

sections.text: 之所以...是因为 — effect first, cause second

Standard order is 因为 X 所以 Y ("because X, so Y"). When you want to lead with the surprising effect and explain it after, flip to 之所以 Y 是因为 X ("the reason Y is because X"). It's a hallmark of essay and op-ed Chinese.

rows.source: 他之所以成功，是因为他从不放弃。
rows.pinyin: Tā zhī suǒ yǐ chénggōng, shì yīnwèi tā cóng bù fàngqì.
rows.translation: The reason he succeeded is that he never gave up.

rows.source: 中国之所以发展迅速，是因为改革开放的政策。
rows.pinyin: Zhōngguó zhī suǒ yǐ fāzhǎn xùnsù, shì yīnwèi gǎigé kāifàng de zhèngcè.
rows.translation: China developed rapidly because of the reform and opening-up policy.

sections.text: 不仅...而且 — "not only... but also"
不仅 X 而且 Y stacks points: not only X, but also Y. The formal form is 不但 X 而且 Y; the literary form 不仅...更 ramps up the second clause.

rows.source: 这部电影不仅获得了好评，而且票房火爆。
rows.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng bùjǐn huòdé le hǎopíng, érqiě piàofáng huǒbào.
rows.translation: This film not only got good reviews but also did huge box office.

rows.source: 他不仅是一位作家，更是一位思想家。
rows.pinyin: Tā bùjǐn shì yí wèi zuòjiā, gèng shì yí wèi sīxiǎngjiā.
rows.translation: He is not only a writer but, even more so, a thinker.

sections.text: Headline grammar
Headlines compress hard. They drop pronouns, particles, and even verbs. Learn these high-frequency journalist verbs and you'll skim headlines in seconds.
据 X 报道 — quick refresher

You met 据报道 at B2, so this is a refresher rather than new ground. At C1, focus on the variants: 据 X 报道 attributes to a named source, while 据悉 ("it is learned") is the unsourced, slightly official cousin. Both anchor the start of a sentence.

rows.source: 据新华社报道，会议将于下周举行。
rows.pinyin: Jù Xīnhuáshè bàodào, huìyì jiāng yú xiàzhōu jǔxíng.
rows.translation: According to Xinhua News Agency, the meeting will be held next week.

rows.source: 据悉，相关部门正在调查此事。
rows.pinyin: Jù xī, xiāngguān bùmén zhèngzài diàochá cǐ shì.
rows.translation: It is learned that the relevant departments are investigating the matter.

Pick the most natural news translation: "The government rolled out a new policy."
Build the headline-style "The two countries signed a trade agreement"
exercises.answer: 两 国 签署 贸易 协议

exercises.prompt: Build "The reason he succeeded is that he never gave up"
exercises.answer: 他 之所以 成功 ， 是因为 他 从不 放弃

exercises.prompt: What does "她之所以受欢迎，是因为她真诚" mean?

The reason she is popular is that she is sincere
She is popular because she pretends

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses 之所以...是因为 correctly?

我之所以是因为学中文喜欢
因为我喜欢中国文化之所以学中文
exercises.answer: 我之所以学中文，是因为我喜欢中国文化

exercises.prompt: Complete: "中国 ___ 发展迅速，是因为改革开放"
exercises.explanation: 之所以 fronts the effect; 是因为 introduces the cause.

exercises.prompt: Build "This plan is not only feasible but also efficient"
exercises.answer: 这个 方案 不仅 可行 而且 高效

exercises.prompt: What does "他不仅是作家，更是思想家" emphasize?
options: Both are true, but the second is the bigger point
exercises.answer: Both are true, but the second is the bigger point
exercises.explanation: 更 ("even more so") amplifies the second clause.

exercises.prompt: Match the connective to its register
Complete: "这本书 ___ 内容丰富，___ 文笔优美" (not only...but also)
Match the political term
What does "加大力度" (jiā dà lì dù) mean in news writing?
exercises.explanation: Common bureaucratic phrase: 加大 (increase) + 力度 (degree of force).

exercises.prompt: Build "The two sides reached an important consensus"
exercises.answer: 双方 达成 了 重要 共识

exercises.prompt: "中美关系" refers to ___ relations
What does "值得深思" (zhí dé shēn sī) signal?
exercises.explanation: Editorial favorite — pushes the reader to take the issue seriously.

exercises.prompt: Match the editorial phrase
Build "This issue cannot be ignored, immediate action is needed"
exercises.answer: 这个 问题 不容 忽视 ， 必须 立即 行动

topics.title: Persuasion & debate
topics.description: Build arguments, concede, refute

guide.intro: Persuasive Chinese has its own choreography: state your premise, acknowledge the counter-argument, then refute. Three structures power the dance — conditionals (要是...就/便, 即使...也), the concessive 虽然...但是, and the rhetorical 难道...吗.

sections.text: Conditionals

rows: As long as X, then Y
除非 X 否则 Y

rows.source: 要是你早点告诉我就好了。
rows.pinyin: Yàoshi nǐ zǎo diǎn gàosù wǒ jiù hǎo le.
rows.translation: If only you had told me earlier.

rows.pinyin: Jíshǐ xiàyǔ, wǒmen yě yào qù.
rows.translation: Even if it rains, we are still going.

rows.source: 只要你努力，就一定会成功。
rows.pinyin: Zhǐyào nǐ nǔlì, jiù yídìng huì chénggōng.
rows.translation: As long as you work hard, you will surely succeed.

rows.source: 除非他道歉，否则我不会原谅他。
rows.pinyin: Chúfēi tā dàoqiàn, fǒuzé wǒ bú huì yuánliàng tā.
rows.translation: Unless he apologizes, I will not forgive him.

sections.text: 虽然...但是 — concede then push back
The strongest debaters concede. 虽然 X 但是 Y ("although X, but Y") signals you've heard the counterpoint and have an answer. Formal upgrade: 尽管 X，然而 Y.

rows.source: 虽然这个方案有风险，但是收益也很大。
rows.pinyin: Suīrán zhège fāng'àn yǒu fēngxiǎn, dànshì shōuyì yě hěn dà.
rows.translation: Although this plan has risks, the returns are also large.

rows.source: 尽管成本上升，然而公司仍然盈利。
rows.pinyin: Jǐnguǎn chéngběn shàngshēng, rán'ér gōngsī réngrán yínglì.
rows.translation: Although costs rose, the company is nevertheless still profitable.

sections.text: 难道...吗 — rhetorical question
难道 ("could it really be that") fronts a question to which the speaker assumes the answer is obvious. Used to challenge an assumption or rebuke.

rows.translation: Could it be that you don't know? (You should know!)

rows.pinyin: Nándào zhè jiù shì dá'àn ma?
rows.translation: Is this really the answer?

sections.text: In writing, balance your concessives. A column that opens with 虽然...但是 and closes with 难道...吗 reads as classic argumentative Chinese.

exercises.prompt: Match the opener
Build "In my view, this view is one-sided"
exercises.answer: 在 我 看来 这个 观点 比较 片面

exercises.prompt: Which is most formal for "I firmly believe"?
exercises.explanation: All four are plausible C1 alternatives, but 坚信 ("firmly believe") is the strongest and most formal — 深信 is close behind, 相信 is neutral, 认定 leans toward "conclude / be convinced".

exercises.prompt: "毫无疑问" (háo wú yí wèn) means ___
Tap the verb of belief you hear
exercises.explanation: 认为 ("hold the view that") states a current belief; 以为 ("used to think / mistakenly thought") implies the speaker has since changed their mind. Mishearing one for the other flips the meaning.

lessons.title: Conditionals — 要是, 即使, 只要

options: 你说得有道理，但是我们也要看到另一面
exercises.answer: 你说得有道理，但是我们也要看到另一面

lessons.description: Sharpen a point with a challenge

options: A genuine question — does he/she know?
exercises.explanation: 难道...吗 expects the answer "of course" or "of course not".

exercises.prompt: Build the rhetorical "Could this really be the only solution?"

exercises.explanation: Rhetorically, the speaker assumes you remember.

topics.title: Chéngyǔ in context
topics.description: Eight high-frequency four-character idioms used the right way

guide.intro: 成语 (chéngyǔ) are four-character idioms that compress a story or principle into one phrase. There are thousands of them, but only a few hundred are actually high-frequency. We'll meet eight that you'll see weekly in news, conversation, and writing — and learn the contexts where each lands well.

sections.text: How idioms slot into sentences

成语 typically work as adjectives, adverbs, or full predicates. Most can stand alone as a four-character verb phrase: 一举两得 ("two birds, one stone") can be the whole verb. Some need a 是 or 的 frame to slot in: 这是一举两得的事.

rows.pinyin: Zhè zhēn shì yì jǔ liǎng dé.
rows.translation: This really is killing two birds with one stone.

rows.pinyin: Tā gōngzuò bàn tú ér fèi.
rows.translation: He gave up halfway through the work.

rows.pinyin: Jǐn shàng tiān huā de shèjì
rows.translation: An icing-on-the-cake design

sections.text: Eight to remember

rows: Win-win solution / two birds, one stone
Help when help is most needed
Enter the village, follow its customs
When in Rome, do as the Romans

sections.text: 锦上添花 vs 雪中送炭
These two are taught as a pair. 锦上添花 is help when things are already good — nice but not vital. 雪中送炭 is help in a crisis — the kind people remember forever. Pick the right one when praising someone.

rows.pinyin: Nǐ zhè shì xuě zhōng sòng tàn, xièxie!
rows.translation: This is help when I really needed it — thank you!

rows.source: 不算什么，只是锦上添花。
rows.pinyin: Bú suàn shénme, zhǐshì jǐn shàng tiān huā.
rows.translation: It's nothing, just a small bonus.

sections.text: Don't pile 成语 on top of 成语. One per paragraph in writing, one per minute in speech. Used sparingly they sound elegant; used densely they sound like a textbook.

topics.title: Abstract & philosophical
topics.description: Talk about ideas, ethics, fate, and meaning

guide.intro: Modern Mandarin still leans on a small cluster of fate-and-cause vocabulary inherited from Confucian, Buddhist, and Daoist thought. Three words do most of the work: 缘分 (fated connection), 因果 (cause and effect), and 命运 (destiny). They aren't religious jargon — speakers use them every day to talk about relationships, outcomes, and choices. Learning the cultural framing keeps you from translating them too flatly.

sections.text: 缘分 — the right people, the right time

缘分 (yuán fèn) names the unseen tie that brings two people, or a person and a place, together. It's used loosely in romance ("we have 缘分"), friendship ("我们很有缘"), and even chance encounters. The Buddhist root is 缘 ("condition that gives rise to a meeting"); the modern register is warm, slightly fatalistic, and very common.

rows.source: 我们能再见面，真是缘分。
rows.pinyin: Wǒmen néng zài jiànmiàn, zhēn shì yuán fèn.
rows.translation: That we could meet again is truly fate.

rows.pinyin: Yǒu yuán qiān lǐ lái xiāng huì.
rows.translation: If fated, even a thousand miles can't keep two from meeting.

rows.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì jiù suí yuán ba.
rows.translation: Let's just let this one go where fate takes it.

sections.text: 因果 — cause and effect

因果 (yīn guǒ) literally pairs 因 (cause) with 果 (fruit / result). In Buddhist usage it names karma; in modern speech it works as a neutral "cause and effect" — useful in argument, science writing, and ethics talk alike. The four-character expression 因果报应 ("karmic retribution") keeps the moral edge.

rows.pinyin: Fán shì dōu yǒu yīn guǒ.
rows.translation: Every event has a cause and an effect.

rows.source: 我们要分析这件事的因果关系。
rows.pinyin: Wǒmen yào fēnxī zhè jiàn shì de yīn guǒ guānxi.
rows.translation: We need to analyse the causal relationship of this matter.

rows.pinyin: Zhòng shàn yīn, dé shàn guǒ.
rows.translation: Plant good causes, reap good fruits.

sections.text: 命运 — destiny you can argue with

命运 (mìng yùn) is destiny, but with more give than the English word suggests. Speakers talk about 改变命运 ("change one's destiny") and 与命运抗争 ("struggle against fate") freely — destiny is fixed enough to name, fluid enough to push against. Adjacent terms: 天命 (heavenly mandate, more solemn), 宿命 (predetermined fate, fatalistic).

rows: Neutral; can be changed in modern usage

sections.text: These words sit in everyday conversation, not just temples. A friend who lands a job they nearly missed will say 这就是缘分; a parent reflecting on a child's path will say 改变命运. Don't over-translate them as "karma" or "fate" — let the context pick the English.

topics.title: Classical echoes (文言)
topics.description: The 之/其/所/而 family — and how they survive in modern formal writing

guide.intro: You will not be writing 文言 (wényán, classical Chinese) — almost no one does. But every Chinese newspaper editorial, legal document, government report, and serious novel is studded with classical particles, fossilized syntax, and four-character compressions that only make sense if you can read the classical underneath. Treat this as the X-ray vision unit.

sections.text: 之 (zhī) — the all-purpose connector

In modern colloquial Chinese 之 is replaced by 的. In formal writing 之 returns: it links a modifier to a noun (爱国之心 — "a heart of patriotism"), substitutes for an object pronoun (取而代之 — "take it and replace it"), and lurks inside dozens of 成语. Whenever you see 之 in a modern text, mentally swap in 的 or "it" and the sentence usually clicks.

rows.translation: What is said has reason — "that has merit."
To sum it up — used to open a closing paragraph.
A treasure of no price — priceless.

sections.text: 其 (qí) — "its / their / the said"

其 is the formal third-person possessive and a gentle determiner. In a contract you will read 其责任 (its/the responsibility). In an editorial: 其原因有三 (the reasons are three). Notice it never takes 的 after it.

rows.translation: In fact (lit. "its truth").
Each gets their proper place.
Among them / within it.

sections.text: 所 (suǒ) — turns a verb into "that which is V-ed"

所 + verb makes a passive-flavored relative clause: 所说 (that which is said), 所做 (that which is done), 所谓 (so-called). Pair it with 的 in modern usage to keep it readable: 我所说的话 — "the words I said." Reporters love this construction.

rows.translation: As is known to all — newspaper opener.
Unprecedented (lit. "never before existed").
The so-called experts — heavy with skepticism.

sections.text: 而 (ér) — "and / yet / and so"

而 fuses two predicates. Coordinative (年轻而有为 — young and capable), adversative (富而不骄 — rich yet not arrogant), or sequential (起而行之 — rise and act). Modern formal speech is full of it: spoken 而 sounds bookish; written 而 sounds polished.

Quick test: if you can replace 而 with English "and", "yet", or "thus" without losing the sense, you've parsed it. If none fit, you're probably looking at the fossilized 然而 (however) or 因而 (therefore).
Other classical fossils still alive

rows: 以…为… ("take X as Y"), 以便, 以免
若…则… ("if…then…"), 否则, 然则
几乎, 在乎, 不亦乐乎
记者, 学者, 读者, 强者
之乎者也 — the cliché of pedantry

sections.text: 之乎者也 (zhī hū zhě yě) is itself an idiom — it means "empty pedantic talk," mocking someone who hides behind classical jargon.

Don't conflate the two 也. Modern 也 is the high-frequency adverb "also / too" (我也去 — "I'm going too"). Classical 也 is a sentence-final marker that functioned roughly as a copula or assertion (… ， … 也 — "… is the case"). Same character, completely different jobs. In the table above, 也 is listed under its classical job; in everyday reading 99% of 也 you'll see is the modern adverb.
Literary number pairs

In literary or written-elevated register, paired numbers function adverbially to mean "a few / scattered." 一二 (yī èr) — "one or two," 三五 (sān wǔ) — "a handful," 七八 (qī bā) — "seven or eight, a small group." These appear in essays, captions, and novels — almost never in speech.

topics.title: Tang poetry foundations
topics.description: 李白, 杜甫, 王维 — the lines every educated speaker can quote

guide.intro: Tang dynasty (618–907) poetry is the cultural reservoir Chinese speakers draw on the way English speakers reach for Shakespeare. You don't need to read every poem — but the half-dozen lines below are quoted in WeChat moments, business toasts, news headlines, and movie titles. Knowing them is the difference between hearing a language and hearing a culture.

sections.text: 李白 — the romantic

Lǐ Bái (701–762), nicknamed 诗仙 (the Poetry Immortal). Famous for moonlit drinking, untethered imagination, and homesickness. His 静夜思 (Quiet Night Thoughts) is the first poem Chinese children memorize.

rows.translation: Before my bed, bright moonlight —
I wondered if it were frost on the ground.
Lifting my head, I gazed at the bright moon —
Lowering it, I thought of my hometown.

sections.text: 故乡 (gù xiāng — hometown) is the most-loaded word in classical Chinese. It still freights modern songs, Lunar New Year speeches, and diaspora literature.

Textual note: the 床前明月光 wording above is the Ming-dynasty redaction (the version every Chinese child memorizes today). The earlier Tang variant reads 床前看月光 / 疑是地上霜 / 举头望山月 / 低头思故乡. If you ever see 看月光 / 望山月 in an academic citation, it isn't a typo — it's the older edition.
杜甫 — the conscience

Dù Fǔ (712–770), 诗圣 (the Poetry Sage). Where Lǐ Bái soars, Dù Fǔ documents — war, hunger, the displaced family. His phrase 国破山河在 ("the nation shattered, mountains and rivers remain") is quoted whenever a country loses something it cannot replace.

rows.translation: The state is broken; the mountains and rivers remain.
Spring in the city — grass and trees grow thick.
Moved by the times, even flowers shed tears.

sections.text: 王维 — the painter-monk

Wáng Wéi (701–761) painted in words and wrote on silk. His couplets are nearly silent: a stream, a bell, a single bird. The phrase 诗中有画，画中有诗 ("poetry in his paintings, paintings in his poetry") was coined to describe him.

rows.translation: Empty mountain — no one in sight.
Only the echo of voices is heard.
Bright moon shines between the pines.

sections.text: 苏轼 — the Song-dynasty bonus

Sū Shì (1037–1101) is technically Song, not Tang, but you cannot graduate without him. His line 但愿人长久，千里共婵娟 ("may we live long and share the moon's beauty across a thousand li") is the standard Mid-Autumn Festival blessing — printed on mooncake boxes nationwide.

rows.translation: May people endure (live long).
And share, across a thousand li, the moon's beauty.

topics.title: Rhetoric and argumentation
topics.description: Parallel structures, hedges, and the rhythm of formal Chinese

guide.intro: Mandarin formal writing has a rhythm. It loves parallel pairs, four-character cadences, and concessive hedges that English would handle with one comma. Internalizing these patterns is what separates the C1 essay ("correct") from the C2 essay ("this could be in 人民日报").

sections.text: Parallel pair: 一方面…另一方面…
"On one hand…on the other…" The skeleton of every balanced opinion piece. The two clauses should be the same length and grammatical shape — that's where Chinese rhetoric earns its style points.

rows.source: 一方面 我们要发展经济，另一方面 也要保护环境。
rows.pinyin: Yì fāngmiàn wǒmen yào fāzhǎn jīngjì, lìng yì fāngmiàn yě yào bǎohù huánjìng.
rows.translation: On one hand we must grow the economy; on the other, we must also protect the environment.

sections.text: Concessive: …也好，…也罢
"Whether X or Y — either way…" A literary, faintly resigned tone. You'll see it in op-eds and novelistic narration. The pair must mirror — same word class, similar length.

rows.source: 成功 也好，失败 也罢，过程 才 重要。
rows.pinyin: Chénggōng yě hǎo, shībài yě bà, guòchéng cái zhòngyào.
rows.translation: Success or failure — what matters is the process.

rows.source: 你 信 也好，不信 也罢，事实 就 在 那里。
rows.pinyin: Nǐ xìn yě hǎo, bú xìn yě bà, shìshí jiù zài nàlǐ.
rows.translation: Believe it or not, the facts are right there.

sections.text: Choice and preference: 与其…不如… / 宁可…也不…
Two paired patterns for ranking options. 与其 X 不如 Y — "rather than X, better Y." 宁可 X 也不 Y — "would rather X than Y." Both are written-register; both make the speaker sound deliberative.

rows.source: 与其 抱怨，不如 行动。
rows.translation: Rather than complain, take action.

rows.source: 他 宁可 辞职，也不 妥协。
rows.pinyin: Tā nìngkě cízhí, yě bù tuǒxié.
rows.translation: He would rather quit than compromise.

sections.text: Discourse shift: 倒是
倒是 (dào shì) — "on the contrary / actually / as it happens." A discourse marker that signals a gentle reversal of expectation. Not the dramatic 反而 — softer, more conversational-formal.

rows.source: 他 平时 话 不多，关键 时刻 倒是 很 果断。
rows.pinyin: Tā píngshí huà bù duō, guānjiàn shíkè dàoshì hěn guǒduàn.
rows.translation: He's usually quiet, but at critical moments he's actually very decisive.

rows.source: 你 这么 一 说，我 倒是 想起来 了。
rows.pinyin: Nǐ zhème yì shuō, wǒ dàoshì xiǎng qǐlái le.
rows.translation: Now that you mention it, I do remember.

sections.text: Building from a premise: 既然…就…
"Given that X, then Y." The premise is treated as agreed-upon — it shifts the conversation forward. Distinct from 因为…所以… (causal) and 如果…就… (hypothetical).

rows.source: 既然 你 已经 决定 了，就 别 再 犹豫。
rows.pinyin: Jìrán nǐ yǐjīng juédìng le, jiù bié zài yóuyù.
rows.translation: Since you've already decided, stop hesitating.

sections.text: Cause-and-effect chain: 之所以…是因为…
"The reason X is because Y." Stylistically inverted from English — Chinese leads with the consequence and only later names the cause. Beloved by editorialists building suspense.

rows.source: 他 之所以 成功，是 因为 他 从 不 放弃。
rows.pinyin: Tā zhī suǒyǐ chénggōng, shì yīnwèi tā cóng bù fàngqì.
rows.translation: The reason he succeeded is that he never gives up.

sections.text: Four-character rhythm rule: when in doubt, balance. 不仅…而且… is fine; 不仅 simple, 而且 ornate sounds wrong. Match the weight of the two clauses and your sentence will sound native.

topics.title: Confucian and Daoist concepts
topics.description: 仁、义、道、无为 — the philosophical vocabulary in modern usage

guide.intro: Modern Mandarin is haunted by two-and-a-half-thousand-year-old conversations. Words like 仁 (rén), 义 (yì), 道 (dào), and 无为 (wú wéi) appear in HR slogans, parenting books, and political speeches — usually drained of their original technical force, but never entirely. To read Chinese deeply you have to feel the philosophical residue.

sections.text: Confucian core: 仁 and 义

仁 (rén) is humaneness — the disposition to treat others as fully human. 义 (yì) is righteousness — doing the right thing even at cost. The compound 仁义 is shorthand for moral character. When a CEO is praised as 有仁义 (yǒu rén yì), they are being called principled, not merely successful.

rows.source: 他 是 一 个 仁义 之 人。
rows.pinyin: Tā shì yí gè rényì zhī rén.
rows.translation: He is a man of humaneness and integrity.

rows.source: 见 利 忘 义
rows.translation: See profit and forget righteousness — chase money and ditch principle.
Give up life to grasp righteousness — die for principle.

sections.text: 礼 — propriety, ritual, manners

礼 (lǐ) is the choreography of how relationships should be enacted — bowing depths, gift weights, who eats first. In modern business, 礼 survives as 礼貌 (politeness), 礼物 (gift), 送礼 (gift-giving), and the everyday verb 失礼 (to be rude / lose face by a breach of manners).

rows.source: 礼 多 人 不 怪
rows.translation: Excessive courtesy is never resented.

rows.source: 来 而 不 往 非 礼 也
rows.pinyin: Lái ér bù wǎng fēi lǐ yě
rows.translation: To receive and not give back is not 礼 — i.e. you must reciprocate.

sections.text: Daoist counterweight: 道 and 无为

道 (dào) is the underlying way of things — natural, ungraspable. 无为 (wú wéi) is "non-coercive action" — accomplishing through alignment rather than force. Modern usage has softened both: 道理 (reason, principle), 知道 (literally "know the way" — the everyday "to know"), 无为而治 (governing by stepping back).

rows.translation: Follow its natural course — let things be.
Govern by non-action — manage by enabling, not directing.
The highest good is like water — yielding, low-seeking, ultimately unstoppable.

sections.text: 上善若水 from the 道德经 is engraved on countless tea-shop walls and tech-CEO LinkedIn bios. Recognize it as Daoist signaling — humility-by-quotation.
中庸 — the middle way

中庸 (zhōng yōng), "the doctrine of the mean," prizes balance over extremes. In modern business and family advice, 中庸之道 (zhōng yōng zhī dào) is the polite phrase for "don't overdo it either way." Speakers reaching for it want to sound measured, even-keeled, philosophically grounded.

rows.source: 我 主张 走 中庸 之 道。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ zhǔzhāng zǒu zhōngyōng zhī dào.
rows.translation: I advocate the middle way.

sections.text: Be careful: 中庸 in younger urban use can be subtly negative — "wishy-washy, refuses to take a side." Read the speaker's tone.

topics.title: Regional language awareness
topics.description: Mainland Putonghua, Taiwan Guoyu, and the Cantonese world

guide.intro: "Chinese" is several languages and several standardizations of one. C2 means you can hear someone speak for ten seconds and tell whether they grew up in Beijing, Taipei, Guangzhou, or Singapore — and adjust your own usage accordingly. You won't speak every variant. You will learn to recognize and respect them.

sections.text: Putonghua vs Guoyu — same language, different standard

Mainland 普通话 (pǔtōnghuà) and Taiwan 国语 (guóyǔ) are the same language with different standardizations: simplified vs traditional characters, mainland Pinyin vs Taiwanese Zhuyin (注音), distinct vocabulary for many modern objects.
On the mainland 土豆 = potato. In Taiwan 土豆 = peanut. This single word has caused decades of dinner-party confusion.
Tone and accent cues

Mainland Putonghua, especially Beijing-flavored, has heavy 儿化音 (érhuàyīn, the rhotic suffix) — 哪儿、玩儿、有点儿. Taiwan Guoyu generally drops 儿化, prefers softer tones, and sounds the neutral tone less aggressively. Southern mainland speakers (Shanghai, Guangzhou) often blur the n/l distinction or merge zh/z, ch/c, sh/s.

rows.translation: Where are you? — Beijing-flavored.
Where are you? — Taiwan / southern / formal.

sections.text: Cantonese — a separate Chinese language

广东话 / 粤语 (Cantonese) is mutually unintelligible with Mandarin in speech, though written Standard Chinese is shared. Cantonese has six tones (some count nine), retains classical Chinese consonant clusters lost in Mandarin, and uses distinct vocabulary: 唔 (m̀h, not) for 不, 佢 (kéuih) for 他, 食 (sihk) for 吃.

rows.translation: Have you eaten? — Cantonese, written informally.

rows.source: 你 吃 了 饭 没有？
rows.pinyin: Nǐ chī le fàn méi yǒu? (Mandarin)
rows.translation: Same question, Mandarin.

sections.text: When you see characters like 嘅、咗、嗮、咩、嘢 in writing — that's written Cantonese (粤文), common on Hong Kong social media but unusual in mainland publications.
Singapore, Malaysia, overseas

Singaporean Mandarin (新加坡华语) is heavily code-mixed with English, Hokkien, and Malay. Vocabulary like 巴刹 (bāshā, market — from Malay pasar) and 德士 (déshì, taxi — from English) is locally standard but invisible on the mainland. Malaysian Chinese communities use similar mixes. Overseas Chinese in the US/Australia often retain pre-1949 vocabulary — 老中 for "older Chinese folks," or older transliterations.
Cross-strait political vocabulary — read the labels

Political register is where word choice tells you the speaker's stance. 大陆 (dàlù, "the mainland") and 内地 (nèidì, "the interior") describe the same territory but signal different framings — 内地 is the term Hong Kong and Macau use within the One-Country framework; Taiwan media usually prefer 中国大陆 or simply 中国. Likewise, 政府 (zhèngfǔ) is neutral "government," while 当局 (dāngjú, "the authorities") is more distanced — used by foreign-press translations and by speakers who want a faintly skeptical tone.

rows: Taiwan media, Hong Kong, overseas Chinese
"The interior" — frames PRC as the inside

sections.text: These choices are not interchangeable. Calling Taiwan's elected government 台湾当局 ("the Taiwan authorities") rather than 台湾政府 is itself a political signal — standard in PRC official media. Reading register includes reading these tells.

A Taiwanese friend says "我爱吃土豆." They probably mean:
exercises.explanation: Mainland 土豆 = potato. In Taiwan, 土豆 = peanut. The same characters; different referent.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is most clearly a mainland register?
exercises.explanation: 地铁 + 坐 is mainland-standard. 捷运 is the Taipei system; 巴士 is Hong Kong / Cantonese for bus.

exercises.explanation: Beijing markers: 今儿 (today, with rhotic), 咱们 (inclusive we, more common in the north), and 玩儿 (rhoticized verb). Compare to flatter southern/Taiwan phrasing.

exercises.explanation: Taiwan markers: 跟你讲 (instead of mainland 跟你说), 有够 (intensifier — distinctively Taiwan), softer sentence-ending 的. The mainland-flavored options use 事儿 with rhotic and 跟你说 / 告诉你.

exercises.prompt: You scroll a Hong Kong forum post: "佢话佢唔嚟喇." This is:
exercises.explanation: 佢, 唔, 嚟, 喇 are Cantonese-specific characters. The Mandarin equivalent: 他说他不来了.

exercises.prompt: Match the Cantonese word to its Mandarin equivalent
Spoken Cantonese and spoken Mandarin are:
options: The same with different vocabulary only
exercises.explanation: They share a writing system (mostly) but the spoken forms are linguistically separate.

exercises.prompt: "我去巴刹买菜。" Where is the speaker most likely from?
exercises.explanation: 巴刹 (bāshā) is from Malay pasar (market). Locally standard in Singapore/Malaysia, almost never heard on the mainland.

exercises.prompt: "德士" (déshì) is the Singapore word for:
exercises.explanation: From English "taxi." Mainland equivalent: 出租车. Taiwan: 计程车.

exercises.prompt: Mainland Mandarin uses 视频 for video; Taiwan uses ___.
An article writes "台湾当局" rather than "台湾政府". This word choice signals:
options: A PRC-aligned framing — distancing the elected government as "the authorities"
An academic term with no political weight
exercises.answer: A PRC-aligned framing — distancing the elected government as "the authorities"
exercises.explanation: 当局 ("the authorities") refuses the term 政府 ("government"). In cross-strait writing it is a standard PRC-state-media tell. Reading register means catching this.

exercises.prompt: A Hong Kong government press release uses "内地" while a Taiwan newspaper uses "中国大陆" for the same territory. Why?
options: Same referent, different framings — 内地 fits a One-Country frame; 中国大陆 keeps explicit distance
They refer to different time periods
exercises.answer: Same referent, different framings — 内地 fits a One-Country frame; 中国大陆 keeps explicit distance
exercises.explanation: Same place, different rhetorical relationship. 内地 ("the interior") presupposes you're inside the same country; 中国大陆 names it as a separate political entity.

topics.title: Media literacy and register
topics.description: Reading newspapers, recognizing propaganda, parsing satire

guide.intro: Reading Chinese news is not just decoding characters — it's reading register. The same event in 人民日报, 财新, BBC中文, 华尔街日报 中文版, and a 微博 satire account will appear in five distinct linguistic costumes. C2 means recognizing the costume.

sections.text: Boilerplate of the official register

Official Chinese reporting has a recognizable lexicon. When you see clusters of the phrases below, you are reading 党媒 (party media) or material that closely echoes it. They are not necessarily false — they are signals of register and stance.

rows: "The relevant authorities" — bureaucratic vagueness, agent unspecified
bù kě gào rén de mùdì
"Ulterior motives" — strong accusation of bad faith
"Hurt the feelings of the X people" — diplomatic outrage marker
"Seek progress while maintaining stability" — economic policy slogan

sections.text: "伤害中国人民的感情" is so formulaic that it has become a Chinese-internet joke. Recognizing the joke is part of recognizing the register.
Hedges of independent reporting

Independent or commercial Chinese-language reporting (财新, 端传媒, 联合早报, BBC中文) tends to use sourced hedges absent from official copy: 据悉, 据知情人士透露, 多名…表示, 截至发稿. These are signals of journalistic register.

rows.pinyin: jù zhī qíng rén shì tòu lù
rows.translation: According to sources familiar with the matter — Wall Street Journal cliché translated wholesale into Chinese.
At the time of publication — used to flag information that might change.
Has not yet responded — neutral phrasing for a no-comment situation.

sections.text: Satire and irony online

Chinese internet culture is famously inventive about evading censorship and signaling irony. Watch for: deliberate typos and homophones ("河蟹" hé xiè, "river crab", for the censored 和谐 héxié, "harmony"); reversed praise ("厉害了，我的国" — originally earnest, often deployed sarcastically now); the bracket-and-comma sneer like 「（笑）」 or 233333 (laughter); and the soft "emmm…" hedge marking polite disagreement.

rows.translation: "Awesome, my country" + "(laughs)" — sarcasm.

rows.pinyin: Zhè bō cāozuò wǒ gěi mǎn fēn
rows.translation: I give this move a perfect ten — almost always sarcastic praise of a misstep.
Those who understand, understand — wink, the censored thing.

sections.text: "懂的都懂" is a strong tell. The writer is naming the unspoken topic without naming it; you're being included in an in-group of readers.
Headline conventions

Chinese-language headlines compress aggressively. Expect colons, slashes, and bracketed labels: 【独家】 (exclusive), 【深度】 (deep dive), 【快讯】 (breaking). The colon often introduces the subject's quote: 张三：我没说过那句话.

topics.title: Formal essay structure (论说文)
topics.description: Openings, transitions, conclusions — the conventions of academic Chinese argument

guide.intro: 议论文 (yìlùnwén) — the argumentative essay — is the dominant academic genre in Chinese high schools, university entrance exams, and editorial pages. It has its own conventions: sourced openings, signposted transitions, weighty conclusions. C2 essay writing means writing inside this scaffold rather than translating English structure into Chinese words.

sections.text: The opening (开篇 kāipiān)

A 议论文 typically opens with one of three moves: a quoted line of classical or canonical authority (借古立论), an observation of a current phenomenon (现象切入), or a counter-position that the writer will then refute (破题). All three are register-marked — the colloquial "let me tell you about a friend of mine…" opener that works in English would feel out of place.

rows.source: 古人云："读万卷书，行万里路." 此言至今仍有 深意。
rows.pinyin: Gǔrén yún: dú wàn juàn shū, xíng wàn lǐ lù. Cǐ yán zhì jīn réng yǒu shēnyì.
rows.translation: The ancients said: "Read ten thousand books, walk ten thousand li." These words still carry deep meaning today.

rows.source: 近年来，人工智能 之 发展 日新月异。
rows.pinyin: Jìnnián lái, réngōng zhìnéng zhī fāzhǎn rìxīnyuèyì.
rows.translation: In recent years, the development of AI has changed by the day. (Phenomenon opener.)

sections.text: Transitions (过渡 guòdù)

Chinese academic writing signals its structure overtly. Each new paragraph typically begins with a connector that names its function: 首先 (first), 其次 (next), 再者 (furthermore), 此外 (besides this), 然而 (however), 反观 (looking conversely at), 综上所述 (summing up the above). Skip these and the essay reads as choppy, no matter how strong each paragraph is on its own.

rows: 首先 / 其次 / 再者
From this we can see — drawing inference
In sum / from all the above — pre-conclusion marker

sections.text: The body argument

Each body paragraph typically follows a 论点-论据-论证 structure: state a thesis-claim (论点), give evidence (论据), explain the reasoning (论证). The evidence is often a citation of a 名人 ("famous figure"), a historical episode, or a contemporary statistic. Hedges like 据统计, 研究表明, 不可否认 and 必须承认 mark the move from claim to evidence.

rows.source: 据统计，超过 七成 的 受访者 表示 …
rows.pinyin: Jù tǒngjì, chāoguò qī chéng de shòufǎngzhě biǎoshì…
rows.translation: Statistics show that over 70 percent of respondents say…

rows.source: 不可否认，问题 之 复杂 远 超 预期。
rows.pinyin: Bù kě fǒurèn, wèntí zhī fùzá yuǎn chāo yùqī.
rows.translation: It cannot be denied that the problem is far more complex than expected.

sections.text: The conclusion (结尾 jiéwěi)

The conclusion is rarely a meek English-style "in conclusion, …". A strong 议论文 ending circles back to the opening (照应开头), restates the thesis with elevated weight, and often closes with a four-character flourish or a forward-looking call. The phrases 综上所述, 由此可见, 总而言之 cue the reader to expect the wrap-up.

rows.source: 综上所述，唯有 持之以恒，方 能 致远。
rows.pinyin: Zōng shàng suǒ shù, wéi yǒu chí zhī yǐ héng, fāng néng zhì yuǎn.
rows.translation: In sum: only with perseverance can one reach far. ("方能" is the elevated form of 才能.)

sections.text: Convention #1 of academic Chinese: prefer the 4-character cadence in your closing line. 持之以恒, 方能致远, 任重道远, 砥砺前行 — these are not clichés, they are tonal closers that signal the essay is ending with weight.

lessons.description: 古人云, 现象切入, and the 破题 move

exercises.prompt: An essay opens with "古人云：\"读万卷书，行万里路.\"" This is which type of opening?
exercises.explanation: 古人云 / 古语有云 / 子曰 — all are signals that the writer is opening with a citation of canonical authority before staking their own thesis.

exercises.prompt: Match the opening type to its function
Build a phenomenon-opener: "In recent years, the development of AI has changed by the day."
exercises.answer: 近年来 人工智能 之 发展 日新月异

lessons.title: Transitions and signposting
lessons.description: 首先 / 其次 / 再者 / 反观 — making structure visible

exercises.prompt: Match the transition to its function
Halfway through an essay, a paragraph begins with "反观西方教育体系…". The writer is signaling:
options: A summary of what was just said
A pivot to a contrasting case used as comparison
exercises.answer: A pivot to a contrasting case used as comparison
exercises.explanation: 反观 = "by contrast / looking conversely at." A standard structural move in 议论文 — pivot to the comparison case to sharpen the thesis.

exercises.prompt: The pre-conclusion marker that means "summing up the above" is ___ (4 characters).
acceptableAnswers: 综上所述 (zōng shàng suǒ shù)
exercises.explanation: 综上所述 cues the reader: the wrap-up paragraph is starting. A near-mandatory move in formal Chinese essays.

lessons.title: Evidence and argument hedges
lessons.description: 据统计 / 研究表明 / 不可否认 / 必须承认

exercises.prompt: Match the hedge to its move in the argument
An essay paragraph reads: "不可否认，问题之复杂远超预期。然而…". The 不可否认…然而… pair functions as:
options: Concession then pivot — "granted X, but Y"
A direct contradiction with no resolution
exercises.answer: Concession then pivot — "granted X, but Y"
exercises.explanation: 不可否认 lets you grant the opposing view's strongest point; 然而 then pivots to your counter-argument. Standard rhetorical move in formal argument.

exercises.prompt: Build: "Statistics show that over 70 percent of respondents are dissatisfied with this policy."
exercises.answer: 据统计 超过 七成 的 受访者 对 此 政策 不 满意

lessons.title: Conclusions with weight
lessons.description: 综上所述, 4-character closers, and 方能 elevation

exercises.prompt: "唯有持之以恒，方能致远." The word 方能 here is the elevated form of:
exercises.explanation: 方能 (fāng néng) is the literary register of 才能 — "only then can." Standard in formal essay closers.

exercises.prompt: Match the 4-character closer to its sense

pairs.right: The burden is heavy and the road long

exercises.prompt: Build a weighty conclusion: "In sum, only with perseverance can one reach far."
exercises.answer: 综上所述 唯有 持之以恒 方能 致远

exercises.prompt: Why do Chinese academic essays often close with a 4-character idiom?
options: It is a tonal convention — the cadence signals the essay is ending with weight
exercises.answer: It is a tonal convention — the cadence signals the essay is ending with weight
exercises.explanation: Convention, not decoration. A C2-fluent essay rounds out with 4-character cadence the same way an English essay might land on a parallel triplet.

topics.title: C2 review — register, idiom, classical, rhythm
topics.description: Mixed-register paragraph parsing, idiom-in-context, register identification, and parallel rewriting

guide.intro: C2 mastery is not knowing one register — it's switching between them in a paragraph and recognizing the switch when someone else does it. This review pulls together classical particles, 成语 in modern context, register identification, and the rhythm of parallel construction.

sections.text: What this review tests

Four lessons, each targeting one C2-level skill: (1) parsing paragraphs that mix classical particles with modern register; (2) identifying which 成语 fits a real headline / news context out of multiple plausible candidates; (3) reading a paragraph and naming its register (official, independent press, satire, literary, academic); (4) recognizing imbalanced parallel constructions and rewriting them so the rhythm holds.
If a question feels like it has two right answers, it usually does — at C2 the test is often "which is more idiomatic / more in-register," not "which is grammatical."

lessons.title: Mixed-register paragraph parsing
lessons.description: Classical particles in modern prose — read, then identify the function

exercises.prompt: A 财新 editorial reads: "众所周知，此次改革之于国民经济，影响深远。然而，其执行之难，前所未有。" Which classical particle is doing the most structural work?
options: 之 — modifier-linker (here connecting nouns into formal phrases)
exercises.answer: 之 — modifier-linker (here connecting nouns into formal phrases)
exercises.explanation: 之于 (relation to), 改革之… (this reform's…), 其执行之难 (the difficulty of its execution). Three uses of 之 carry the editorial register.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase from the editorial above to its function

pairs.left: 此次改革之于国民经济
pairs.right: 之于 — X's relation to Y
